draft.title: The New Deal
card: The New Deal was a set of programs begun by President Franklin Roosevelt from 1933. Its aim was to fight the Great Depression in the United States.
Roosevelt used government spending to create jobs. Public works programs paid unemployed people to build roads, bridges and parks.

New agencies were set up to deal with particular problems. For example, the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation protected bank savings, and the Social Security Act of 1935 gave support to older people.
The New Deal eased hardship and restored confidence in banks. Unemployment fell but stayed high, and the economy recovered fully only later.
draft.remember: The New Deal used government spending and new agencies to ease the Depression, but it did not end it alone.

a.q: Which action is an example of the New Deal's approach?
opts: Paying unemployed people to build public roads
Leaving the economy to recover without any help
Raising taxes to cut government spending
Ending bank accounts to stop people losing savings
a.why: The New Deal used government spending to create jobs, such as building roads. Leaving the economy alone is the opposite approach, and cutting spending would not have created work.
a.clue: Look for government spending that creates jobs.

b.q: In 1934, Dana in Ohio feared her bank would fail and her savings would vanish. Which New Deal measure was meant to ease this fear?
opts: The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation
The Social Security Act
A public works road program
A rise in income taxes
b.why: The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation protected bank savings, which restored confidence in banks. The Social Security Act is a tempting answer, but it supported older people rather than bank savers.
b.clue: Which agency was set up to protect savings?

a.best: Paying unemployed people to build public roads

problems.detail: The card calls the Social Security Act of 1935 an example of a new agency. It was a law, not an agency; it set up the Social Security Board. Students may come away thinking the Act itself was an agency.

The clue ('Which agency was set up to protect savings?') nearly restates the card's line that the FDIC 'protected bank savings'. It also points to the only option that is an agency, so it gives the answer away rather than prompting thought.

check.summary: The facts check out and both questions have one clear right answer. The card wrongly calls the Social Security Act an agency, and question b's clue all but gives the answer away.

proposal.title: The New Deal
card: The New Deal was a set of programs begun by President Franklin Roosevelt in 1933. Its aim was to fight the Great Depression in the United States.
Roosevelt used government spending to create jobs. Public works programs paid unemployed people to build roads, bridges and parks.
New agencies dealt with particular problems. The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) insured bank savings, so a bank failure no longer wiped them out. This restored trust in banks.
New laws also helped, such as the Social Security Act of 1935, which set up pensions for older people. Unemployment fell but stayed high, and full recovery came only later.
proposal.remember: The New Deal used government spending, new agencies and new laws to ease the Depression, but it did not end it alone.

a.q: Which action is an example of the New Deal's approach?
opts: Paying unemployed people to build public roads
Leaving the economy to recover without any help
Raising taxes to cut government spending
Cutting relief payments to balance the budget
a.why: The New Deal used government spending to create jobs, such as building roads. Leaving the economy alone is the opposite approach, and cutting spending or relief would not have created work.
a.clue: Did the New Deal spend more or less?

b.q: In 1934, Dana in Ohio feared her bank would fail and her savings would vanish. Which New Deal measure was meant to ease this fear?
opts: Government insurance of bank deposits
Government pensions for older people
Paying jobless people to build roads
A rise in income taxes on the rich
b.why: The FDIC insured bank deposits, so savers would not lose their money if a bank failed. Pensions from the Social Security Act are tempting, but they supported older people, not bank savers.
b.clue: What would stop a bank failure costing Dana her money?

a.best: Paying unemployed people to build public roads
